issues.claim: The FCS is an Australian Government-backed safety net
issues.evidence: Live page: "The Financial Claims Scheme (FCS) is an Australian Government scheme." The phrase "government-backed safety net" comes from a different page (https://www.apra.gov.au/apra-explains-financial-claims-scheme); meaning is equivalent.
issues.suggested_fix: The Financial Claims Scheme (FCS) is an Australian Government scheme that provides protection for depositors of banks, credit unions and building societies

issues.claim: can be activated in the unlikely event that an ADI fails
issues.evidence: "The FCS can be activated by the Australian Government in the unlikely event that an ADI or general insurer fails." "Once activated, the FCS will be administered by APRA."

issues.claim: each holder's share is then added to their other deposits at the same ADI
issues.evidence: "Each account holder's share is then added to any other eligible deposits they may hold under their own name" (minor: page says 'eligible' deposits)
issues.suggested_fix: each account holder's share is then added to any other eligible deposits they hold under their own name at the same ADI

issues.claim: List of covered accounts
issues.evidence: Chunk list is a subset of the page list. Page also lists current accounts, debit card accounts, personal basic accounts, farm management deposit accounts, pensioner deeming accounts and retirement savings accounts; excluded also 'nostro'/'vostro' accounts of foreign corporations. Optional completeness addition.

issues.claim: Payments are made ... by cheque or electronically to another account nominated by the account holder
issues.evidence: "In most cases FCS payment would be made either by cheque or electronically to an alternate account"; "Payments will only be made in Australian dollars." Missing qualifier 'in most cases' (certain prescribed accounts are transferred to a same-kind account at another institution).
issues.suggested_fix: Payments are only made in Australian dollars and, in most cases, by cheque or electronically to an alternate account nominated by the account holder.

issues.claim: To recover amounts above the $250,000 limit, the account holder must make a claim in the institution's liquidation
issues.evidence: "an account-holder making a claim to recover an amount over the FCS limit of $250,000 would rank third" in the liquidation priority. Page does not use 'must'; useful condition omitted: such claims rank third and recovery is not guaranteed.
issues.suggested_fix: An account holder can make a claim in the institution's liquidation to recover an amount over the $250,000 FCS limit; such claims rank third in priority.

issues.claim: Under the Privacy Act's Australian Privacy Principles, as explained by the OAIC, an organisation ... must give a person access
issues.evidence: The page body does not refer to the Privacy Act or explain the APPs; it only links to 'Australian Privacy Principles Guidelines, Chapter 12'. It says: "Australian privacy law gives you a general right to access your personal information" ... "except where the law allows them to refuse your request."
issues.suggested_fix: The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) says Australian privacy law gives you a general right to access your personal information, except where the law allows an organisation to refuse your request.

issues.claim: An organisation may charge for giving access, but it cannot use the charge to discourage requests
issues.evidence: "An organisation can't use this charge to discourage you from requesting access"; missing condition: the charge "can't be excessive" and making the request itself is free.
issues.suggested_fix: An organisation may charge for giving access, but the charge can't be excessive and can't be used to discourage you from requesting access.

issues.claim: If it refuses access, it must explain its reasons and how the person can make a complaint
issues.evidence: "tell you in writing their reasons for refusing and how you can make a complaint" - chunk omits 'in writing'.
issues.suggested_fix: If it refuses access, it must tell the person in writing its reasons for refusing and how they can make a complaint.

issues.claim: If an organisation refuses to correct ... ask it to attach a statement
issues.evidence: Page: may ask it to "associate a statement"; it "must take reasonable steps to associate the statement with your personal information". Omitted: the organisation must explain its reasons in writing, and the person can complain.

issues.claim: some privacy complaints about banks may need to go to AFCA
issues.evidence: Page (updated 2 March 2026): for a privacy complaint about a bank you "should contact the Australian Financial Complaints Authority"; AFCA "has the power to deal with your privacy complaint". Page is more direct than the chunk.
issues.suggested_fix: For a privacy complaint about a bank, the OAIC says you should contact the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), which has the power to deal with your privacy complaint.

issues.claim: An organisation that suspects a breach has 30 days to assess it
issues.evidence: Page does not mention 'suspects' and qualifies the period with 'Generally' and states what is assessed: "Generally, an organisation or agency has 30 days to assess whether a data breach is likely to result in serious harm." The 'suspected breach' framing comes from the research notes, not this page.
issues.suggested_fix: Generally, an organisation or agency has 30 days to assess whether a data breach is likely to result in serious harm.

issues.claim: A notification includes the organisation's contact details, the kinds of information involved, a description of the breach, and recommended steps
issues.evidence: Notification "should include": name and contact details, "the kinds of personal information involved in the breach", "a description of the data breach", "recommendations for the steps you can take in response".

issues.claim: can ask the credit provider, such as the bank, or any credit reporting body to correct it
issues.evidence: Page advises to "contact the relevant credit provider in the first instance"; credit reporting bodies can also be asked. Ordering nuance omitted.
issues.suggested_fix: contact the relevant credit provider (such as the bank) in the first instance, or ask a credit reporting body to correct it

issues.claim: During a ban, the credit reporting body generally cannot use or disclose the person's credit report without their written consent
issues.evidence: "a credit reporting body mustn't use or disclose your consumer credit report" except "if you've consented, in writing" or "an Australian law or a court or tribunal order require" it. Also: ban lasts "21 days after you first make the request"; request and extensions are free.

issues.claim: The Scams Prevention Framework Act was passed in 2025
issues.evidence: Not stated on the 9 June 2026 media release. Source is the Treasury release of 13 Feb 2025 (https://ministers.treasury.gov.au/ministers/stephen-jones-2022/media-releases/parliament-passes-world-leading-scams-prevention).
issues.suggested_fix: Remove, or move to a chunk whose url is the 13 February 2025 Treasury release.

issues.claim: banking was among the first sectors designated
issues.evidence: Not stated on this page (it only lists the sectors AFCA can handle disputes in). Source is the 28 May 2026 release (https://ministers.treasury.gov.au/ministers/daniel-mulino-2025/media-releases/albanese-government-steps-industry-protections-stop).
issues.suggested_fix: Remove, or cite the 28 May 2026 Treasury release.

issues.claim: Most framework obligations start on 31 March 2027, so as at October 2026 they are not yet in force
issues.evidence: Page gives no commencement date; it only says "Once operational". Date comes from the ACCC SPF page (https://www.accc.gov.au/about-us/scams-prevention-framework) and the 28 May 2026 release.
issues.suggested_fix: Remove, or split into a separate chunk sourced from the 28 May 2026 Treasury release ("ready for 31 March next year").

issues.claim: Consumers must first try to resolve the dispute with the business
issues.evidence: "Where disputes cannot be resolved directly with businesses, consumers can escalate matters to AFCA."

issues.claim: The Consumer Data Right (CDR), known in banking as open banking
issues.evidence: The page does not mention 'open banking'. It says: "The Consumer Data Right allows you to give an accredited business access to your consumer data".
issues.suggested_fix: The Consumer Data Right allows you to give an accredited business access to your consumer data. (Keep 'open banking' only in tags, or cite a page that uses the term.)

issues.claim: opt-in; available in banking; withdraw consent at any time; ask for deletion if no longer needed
issues.evidence: "The Consumer Data Right is an opt-in system." "It's available in the banking sector." "you can withdraw your consent at any time" "You can ask for your data to be deleted if it is no longer needed."

issues.claim: People affected by identity theft, scams or cyber incidents can call the individual helpline
issues.evidence: Page: "National identity and cyber support service"; individual helpline 1800 595 160, Monday to Friday, 7am to 7pm AEST. Page frames individual support around identity theft/scams and cyber incidents for sole traders/small business.
